fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. The kings of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites and the rest came together to wage war against Joshua and Israel. The list runs from the hill country all the way to the coast. Getting that many kings to agree on anything is a miracle. I can't even get a group chat to pick a movie.

Right, baker. Their whole supply of bread was dry and moldy. Fresh and soft would have ruined the look they were going for. Even the stalest cookie I ever pressed would have been fresher than that sack.

No shooing here, friend. The men of Israel ask, “Perhaps you dwell near us. How can we make a treaty with you?” They don't send anyone off. They poke at the story first. I think those words sound like Israel isn't sure yet.

Close, friend, but look at what they actually say to Joshua. They talk about Egypt, and about Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites beyond the Jordan. Jericho and Ai don't come up in that speech. Those two cities show up back in verse 3, as the news the Gibeonites had heard.

Yes, baker. They say their clothes and sandals are “…worn out from our very long journey.” Cracked wineskins, patched sandals and threadbare clothes are what they wanted Joshua to see. The distance behind that picture was not true (Joshua 9:16). It's a very convincing look for a trip that never happened.

Yes, baker. Joshua made a treaty of peace with them to let them live. Right before that, the men of Israel sampled their provisions but did not seek the counsel of the LORD. The leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them too. That treaty is going to matter.

No spies in this scene, friend. The text says the men of Israel sampled their provisions, and then Joshua made a treaty of peace with them to let them live. Sending anyone out never comes up in the passage.

That's right, baker. The leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them, too. So the treaty had Joshua's agreement and the leaders' oath behind it. Keep an eye on that oath, because it matters a lot.

Right, baker. Three days after the treaty, the Israelites learned that the Gibeonites were neighbors, living among them. The faraway land was a story they told. A very long journey that ends up next door is quite a trip.

That's not what happens, friend. Israel reaches the cities, but the Israelites did not attack them. The leaders had sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. The whole congregation grumbled against the leaders, but the oath is the reason the text gives.

Yes, baker. The Israelites did not attack them. The text gives the reason: the leaders had sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. The congregation grumbled against the leaders, but no attack came.

That's the job, baker. The leaders say, “Let them live, but let them be woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation.” They keep their promise to let the Gibeonites live. Wood and water are chores like laundry: finished today, needed again tomorrow.

Yes, baker. Joshua asks why they deceived him by saying they lived far away when they lived among Israel. Then he tells them they are under a curse and will perpetually serve as woodcutters and water carriers for the house of his God. He says it plainly. I think this part is heavy.

Not a blessing, friend. Joshua asks why they deceived him, and then he tells them they are under a curse. That curse comes with a lasting job as woodcutters and water carriers for the house of his God.

That's what they say, baker. They tell Joshua they were told the LORD commanded His servant Moses to give Israel all the land. So, in their words, “…we greatly feared for our lives because of you…” That fear is the reason they give for the trick.

The text doesn't say anything about spying, friend. The Gibeonites say they were told the LORD commanded His servant Moses to give Israel all the land, and that is why they feared for their lives. Fear is the reason they give, and spying never comes up.

That's not what they tell Joshua, friend. They say they were told the LORD commanded His servant Moses to give Israel all the land and wipe out its inhabitants. So, in their words, they greatly feared for their lives. Taking land isn't the reason they give.
